replies:
Good — final round prep for Lincoln International analyst role. Tell me one thing first: is this an in-person on-site or a virtual final? If you don't answer, I'll assume virtual.

Prep in the room (what you must show), quick plan, and three tailored practice questions with model answers you can adapt. Then one thing for you to do now.
What to show in the final round (short, direct)
- Transaction orientation: demonstrate you can move a deal forward — highlight specific, recent deal work or modeling you did, what you produced, and the next decision it enabled. Be concrete: dates, numbers, outputs.
- Technical competence: be fluent on LBO basics, comps, accretion/dilution, and how your model links (inputs → outputs). You must be able to walk through a one-page model in 2–3 minutes.
- Commercial judgment: explain why a buyer would pay X for a target — use valuation anchors (synergies, multiples, growth, margin assumptions).
- Fit and stamina: show you’ll do long hours and client-facing work — short examples of tight-deadline delivery and handling senior stakeholders.
- Attention to detail: proofs, clean slides, precise answers; when asked a math or modeling question, narrate your steps.
Short plan for the next 48 hours
1) Decide whether it's virtual or onsite (your call). If virtual, test camera/mic and screen sharing. If onsite, plan travel and arrive 30–45 min early.
2) Prepare one recent deal/example you own end-to-end (30–60 sec pitch + 90–120 sec deep dive).
3) Rehearse 6–8 technical answers and one 7–10 minute mock presentation of a model or slide.
4) Prepare 3 thoughtful questions for interviewers (see examples below).
5) Rest well the night before; final rounds are often sequential — energy matters.
Three targeted practice questions + model answers (use your specifics)
1) "Walk me through a recent financial model you built — what were the key assumptions and outcome?"
Model answer (structure: context → action → result):
- Context: "I modeled a $[size] sale of [target type] to [buyer type] to evaluate an exit at different multiples."
- Action: "I built an operating model with revenue drivers (volume, price), margin steps to Adjusted EBITDA, then a 5-year DCF and exit multiples. Key assumptions were revenue CAGR [x%], margin expansion of [y]pts driven by [cost saves]. I stress‑tested sensitivity to margin and exit multiple."
- Result: "Base case IRR was [x]%, buyer willing to pay up to [multiple]x EV/EBITDA for 20% accretion; the sensitivity showed the deal only works if EBITDA margin improves by ≥[z] pts. I recommended we prioritize cost-synergy initiatives in diligence."
One concrete improvement when you practice: swap generic numbers for the real ones you used.
2) Technical: "How do you think about valuation for a mid-market family-owned business?"
Model answer (structure: framework → specifics):
- Framework: "Use trading comps, precedent transactions and DCF; weight comps and transactions more for synergies and control premium, DCF for standalone cash generation."
- Specifics: "In mid-market, comps are noisy; use local/regional comps, adjust for size discount and owner-operator premium, and analyze transaction multiples for control premiums (~20–30% typical). For cash flow conversion, normalize owner compensation and add back one‑time costs."
Practice improvement: cite one example assumption you'll normalize (owner salary, related-party revenue).
3) Behavioral: "Tell me about a time you found an error in work before it went to a client. What did you do?"
Model answer (STAR, with metric):
- Situation: "On a sell‑side process we had a 30‑slide CIM due in 24 hours."
- Task: "I discovered a revenue line tied to a spreadsheet link that was double-counting a contract."
- Action: "I isolated the link, corrected the formula, reran the model, and flagged the change to the senior banker with an email noting the impact."
- Result: "The corrected CIM reduced projected revenue 1Q by 8%, avoiding an overstatement to buyers; the team caught an additional data gap because of my note and we delivered on time."
When you practice: quantify the impact (time saved, % correction) with your real numbers.

Three interviewer questions you should have ready (choose 2–3)
- "What's a recent mid-market deal Lincoln sourced that surprised the team, and why?"
- "How do analysts interact with senior bankers on live processes here?"
- "What are the most common mistakes new analysts make in diligence at Lincoln?"
Quick technical checklist (2–3 mins before any technical interview)
- Open Excel file with a simple 3-statement model and a sensitivity tab.
- Have a one-page note with your deal example (context, key assumptions, one lesson) visible.
- Bring calculator and a pen for mental math prompts.
- If virtual: share full-screen Excel window and test giving control.

One mock now
I'll ask the first question for a timed mock: "Walk me through a recent financial model you built — what were the key assumptions and outcome?" Answer in 90–150 seconds as you would in the room; I'll score it and give one concrete fix, then the next question.

Is this virtual or onsite? (If you skip, I’ll assume virtual.)
